title: Because TESO Asks, Does That Mean It Has No Strength?
translatorNote: This translation is intended to carry Kalaignar's voice into clear, contemporary English rather than recast the letter as literary or academic prose. It preserves the source's argument, political directness, rhetorical questions, repetition, irony, factual detail, and paragraph order. Names, dates, figures, quotations, and intentional English expressions are retained. Where Tamil idiom cannot be reproduced literally without sounding unnatural, the English follows its sense and rhetorical force without adding claims absent from the source. The original Tamil is reproduced in full below the translation and remains the authoritative text. `Udanpirappē` is retained in Tamil transliteration rather than flattened into “brother,” “sister,” or “comrade.” Literally evoking “one born alongside me,” Kalaignar uses it as a distinctive address of shared identity, equality, affection, and solidarity within the movement. Letter-specific notes: 1. The translation preserves the source's distinction between supporting the U.S. resolution, strengthening it through amendments, and TESO's separate demand that India itself advance a stronger international-investigation/referendum initiative. 2. `முழு அடைப்புப் போராட்டம்` is rendered as **shutdown** in the quoted criticism; the surrounding TESO mobilisation remains described as a general strike/protest according to context. 3. The Bandaranaike–Chelvanayakam, Dudley–Chelvanayakam and Rajiv Gandhi–Jayewardene agreements are named exactly at the level of the source, without outside historical expansion. 4. Claims about international support, the number of supporting countries, Sri Lankan responses and alleged war crimes remain attributed to Kalaignar and the actors he cites; no external verification is imported into this archival translation.
paragraphs: For the protection of the welfare of the Eelam Tamils, we reconstituted TESO with me as its President and DMK General Secretary Perasiriyar, K. Veeramani, Thol. Thirumavalavan, Suba. Veerapandian and Subbulakshmi Jagadeesan as members. From time to time we discussed in detail the many issues concerning what the letter describes as genocide of the Tamil people in Sri Lanka, human-rights violations, war crimes and Sinhalisation; we passed appropriate resolutions and sent them to the Government of India.

We did not stop there. We invited representatives of several countries and leaders of political parties in India, obtained their views, framed fourteen resolutions and adopted them unanimously at the great TESO conference held in Chennai on 12 August 2012. Our DMK Members of Parliament personally gave those resolutions to Prime Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh and supplied the necessary explanations.

Later, DMK Treasurer Thalapathi Thambi M.K. Stalin and DMK parliamentary party leader Thambi T.R. Baalu took the resolutions to New York and Geneva, personally submitted them at the headquarters of the United Nations and at the U.N. human-rights body, and provided the necessary details and basic supporting material.

As a continuation, we formed teams of our Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha members, had them visit the embassies of various countries in Delhi, directly presented the TESO conference resolutions and sought those countries' support.

On 8 February, on behalf of TESO, we held a massive black-shirt protest in Chennai under my leadership. The purpose of that demonstration was to demand that Sinhala-majoritarian President Rajapaksa be declared an international war criminal and to draw the world's attention to the killing by the Sinhala military of Balachandran, the young son of Liberation Tigers leader Velupillai Prabhakaran. On 5 March TESO conducted a siege protest in front of the Sri Lankan mission in Chennai. Many thousands of comrades participated and were arrested. On 7 March, in India's capital Delhi, we held a TESO seminar on the cruelties being inflicted on Eelam Tamils.

On behalf of the DMK, we sought debates in both Houses of Parliament on the Eelam Tamil issue. During those debates leaders of all parties argued strongly along lines close to the DMK's position. But replying for the Union Government, Hon'ble External Affairs Minister Salman Khurshid said:

“At the U.N. Human Rights Council meeting in Geneva, after the Sri Lankan government holds talks with the United States regarding the resolution being brought by the United States, the Government of India will decide whether or not to support that resolution.”
But the Sri Lankan government rejected this Indian suggestion. Ravinatha Aryasinha, speaking for Sri Lanka, declared:

“Our country does not intend to hold talks with the United States. Sri Lanka completely rejects the substance of the U.S. resolution. A visit by U.N. observers to a country must take place with the consent or at the invitation of the country concerned.”

We cannot understand on what basis those in the Union Government believed that Sri Lanka would accept India's advice. How could they have forgotten the lesson the Sinhala government has been teaching India for so long? Sri Lanka disregarded the Bandaranaike–Chelvanayakam agreement, the Dudley–Chelvanayakam agreement and the Rajiv Gandhi–Jayewardene agreement. It humiliated Pandit Nehru and young leader Rajiv Gandhi. Yet India continues to call Sri Lanka a friendly country and seems intent on protecting it. That remains a source of pain we cannot understand. Even so, we still have hope that at least at the last moment India will support the U.S. resolution.

Now that Sri Lanka has rejected without even being willing to consider the advice given by India with such confidence, the question still remains: when will the Union Government firmly announce its position on the U.S. resolution before the U.N. Human Rights Council?

In this situation, some say that the draft resolution on Sri Lanka submitted by the United States at the ongoing Geneva meeting will not benefit the Eelam Tamils and contains nothing severe enough to punish Sri Lanka. Like certain newspapers that repeatedly fall over themselves to support the ruling AIADMK in Tamil Nadu, directly or indirectly, some politicians have also announced that the TESO-sponsored shutdown “fizzled out,” merely to show that they too “exist.”

Because TESO, of which the DMK is a part, has been continuously pressuring India to support the U.S. resolution, some people in Tamil Nadu, out of hostility, speak as though that resolution contains nothing at all. Tamils around the world are watching them.
TESO has never declared that the American resolution is itself completely firm, final or sufficiently severe. Even so, there are basic reasons why TESO asks India to support it.

When no other country has come forward to move any resolution in the United Nations, the common forum of the world's nations, against the Sri Lankan government that the letter accuses of crushing and destroying the Eelam Tamils, we should welcome the fact that a great power, the United States, has taken the opportunity to bring one. It was because the United States brought the resolution last time that it was adopted. This time too, a majority of member countries of the U.N. Human Rights Council have expressed support for the American resolution.

At a forum common to all the nations of the world, it was the United States that initiated the first move against Sri Lanka. That move itself has created concern and sympathy around the world for the Eelam Tamil issue, and shock and fear in the Sinhala government of Sri Lanka. Tamils around the world themselves acknowledge this.

TESO has no direct opportunity to propose a resolution against Sri Lanka in the United Nations. The same is true of every political party here. That is why, on behalf of TESO, we have continuously raised our voice and submitted demands that there should be a strong resolution for a credible, independent international investigation into Rajapaksa's alleged war crimes and human-rights violations, including genocide of the Tamil people; that India itself should take a separate resolution before the U.N. Human Rights Council for a general referendum so that dawn may come in the lives of the Eelam Tamils; and that, at the very least, India should support the resolution brought by the United States with appropriate amendments.

In today's situation, when we say pressure must be exerted both for support of the American resolution and for India to bring a separate resolution, some politicians here should think deeply: can we ourselves move a resolution in the assembly of the world's nations? Can we ourselves directly set a deadline for Sri Lanka? Can we ourselves raise an army and call Sri Lanka to war?

If these few politicians who constantly express views about the Eelam Tamils can formulate a higher and more appropriate position than the one TESO has now adopted, both Eelam Tamils and Tamils around the world will welcome it with joy.

At a time when a great power such as the United States comes forward on its own to move a resolution against Sri Lanka, and when more than thirty countries are prepared to support it, should we not at least welcome that? It is with that thought—and because, even if the sufferings of the Eelam Tamils cannot immediately be wiped away completely, this can at least give them some consolation—that TESO welcomes the United States bringing the resolution and asks the Government of India to come forward to support it with suitable amendments.

But some people here seem to imagine that they themselves are mighty “superpowers.” As though their role is to find fault with everything, they say that this is wrong and that is wrong in the American resolution and make needless criticisms, trying to muddy the waters!
With affection, M.K. 14 March 2013
